sections.history: Cheranmahadevi is an old market town on the Tamiraparani, some twenty-odd kilometres west of Tirunelveli on the road to Ambasamudram. Its Shiva temple, the shrine of Ammainathar on the riverbank, is the second of the Nava Kailasam and the one linked with the Moon; in the round of nine it is often simply called the Kailasanathar of Cheranmahadevi. The temple's long story reaches back into the Pandya country's past, and it was renovated in the time of the Chola emperor Kulothunga I, in the late eleventh or early twelfth century, when the far south lay within the Chola realm. It remains a quiet village temple, cared for by the town that grew up around it.
sections.architecture: The temple is a modest Dravidian stone shrine facing the river. Its arrangement holds a surprise: the Goddess Avudai Ammal has her own shrine to the right of the lord's sanctum, a placement seldom seen in the south. Among the pillars of the mandapa, one carries a carving of two women pounding and winnowing paddy — the temple's founding story set in stone. The sacred tree is a banyan, and the Tamiraparani itself is the temple's tirtham, reached by the bathing steps below.
sections.legends: The temple's own story is of two sisters, devout and poor, who earned their living by husking paddy and selling rice. Their lingam stood without a roof, and they set aside a little each day to build it a shelter. One evening Shiva came to them as a hungry brahmin; while he ate, the lamp went out, and the sisters lit a wick in a coconut shell so that he could finish his meal. Offered a boon, they asked only that he help build the temple — and from that day prosperity came to them. Devotees still offer a coconut lamp and rice here in remembrance.
sections.festivals: The celestial wedding, Thirukalyanam, is celebrated in the Tamil month of Aippasi, and Maha Shivaratri and the monthly pradosham are kept with devotion. As the Moon's shrine of the Nava Kailasam, the temple also draws pilgrims on Mondays and full-moon days. Confirm dates locally.
sections.experience: The coconut-shell lamp is the gesture that belongs to this temple: a small flame offered as the sisters once offered theirs, beside a handful of rice. Cheranmahadevi is the second stop of the Nava Kailasam, between Papanasam upstream and Kodaganallur downstream, and its riverside setting makes it a gentle pause on the day-long round.

visit.timings: Open daily with morning and evening darshan sessions and a midday closure, as at most village temples of the region. Confirm current timings locally before visiting.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional dress is expected — shoulders and knees covered; footwear removed before entering. Men are traditionally asked to remove the upper garment before the sanctum, as at many southern shrines; follow the posted rules.
visit.photography: Photography is restricted in and around the sanctum; follow the posted rules and the priests' guidance.
visit.gettingThere: Cheranmahadevi lies in Tirunelveli district, about 22–24 km west of Tirunelveli on the road to Ambasamudram and Papanasam, with frequent buses. Cheranmahadevi railway station is on the Tirunelveli–Tenkasi line; Thoothukudi is the nearest airport.
